validity.recommendation: no existence/classification/status action needed; note chronic low utilization in ResearcherNotes
validity.researcher_notes: EXISTENCE: unambiguous. Confirmed via the original FERC certificate docket CP09-54 (Federal Register Notice of Application, filed Jan 27, 2009 by Ruby Pipeline, L.L.C.), EIA's Historical Natural Gas Pipeline Projects dataset (row 'Ruby Pipeline Project', Docket CP09-54, Regulatory Agency FERC, Status 'Completed', in-service 2011-07-28), Wikipedia, and a current (issued/effective June 10, 2026) FERC Gas Tariff filed by 'Ruby Pipeline, L.L.C.' that repeatedly references 'the Docket No. CP09-54-000 facilities' -- proving this is a live, actively-tariffed FERC asset today, not a phantom/GEM-only entry. CLASSIFICATION: correctly transmission/interstate gas, not gathering -- 683-mile, 42-inch interstate mainline with FERC-jurisdictional tariff, multiple receipt/delivery interconnects (Opal Hub area and Malin-area interconnects per the tariff's point tables). DUPLICATE: checked against the full 46-row roster -- no other row shares this Opal(WY)-to-Malin(OR) route; not a duplicate of Cheyenne Plains/Cheyenne Connector/Kern River/Mojave/GTN or any other West-batch pipeline. STATUS: 'operating' is correct and current, but the batch brief's own flag (post-bankruptcy reduced service) is real and worth recording: Ruby has been chronically underutilized since shortly after start-up (NGI, 2011: initial flows only 4.3% of the 1.5 Bcf/d design capacity) and remains so today -- Wikipedia states roughly 50% utilization 'as of 2026', while an independent midstream-analyst source (East Daley Analytics) states 2025 throughput averaged only 208 MMcf/d, i.e. ~14% of capacity, attributing the weakness to competing Canadian gas imports into the Pacific Northwest. Both sources agree the line is NOT idled or converted -- it continues interstate FIRM/interruptible transportation service under its live FERC tariff -- so this is a utilization caveat, not a status change. Citation-pool coverage: of the 16 harvested wiki citations, I opened/resolved bit.ly/2kFqoiK (-> en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruby_Pipeline), prnewswire.com (bankruptcy filing), and attempted reuters.com (401 bot-wall, unresolved -- archive.org's CDX API was itself rate-limited (429) for the whole session so no Wayback fallback could be tried) and businesswire.com x2 + blankrome.com (403/429 bot-walls; blankrome's response body was a Vercel bot-checkpoint page, not the article, on every retry). eia.gov/naturalgas/data.php is a generic landing page (not pipeline-specific) so I used the more specific eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=3210 article and the EIA pipeline-projects workbook instead. kindermorgan.com's 2018-vintage Ruby page and blm.gov's project page were not opened -- deprioritized once independent corroboration for every data point was already in hand from other sources; neither is needed to support or contradict any value here.

validity.recommendation: update Owner1 to 'Tallgrass Energy' (Owner1% stays 100.00%) -- Ruby Pipeline LLC is the asset-holding SPV, not a corporate owner, and its parent has changed twice since the current entry was last touched
validity.researcher_notes: Owner1 = 'Ruby Pipeline LLC [100%]' is the SAME defect pattern the batch brief flags for P0151 Alliance: an operating/holding-entity name sitting in the Owner slot rather than the corporate owner. 'Ruby Pipeline, L.L.C.' is genuinely real -- it is the FERC certificate-holder and tariff-filer (see the Operator fill below) -- but it has never been an independent company; it has always been wholly owned by a rotating cast of corporate parents: El Paso Corporation (2009 FERC application, 100%) -> a 50/50 JV structure after El Paso brought in a partner during construction (SEC 8-K, El Paso Pipeline Partners, 2010) -> Kinder Morgan inherited El Paso's share when KM acquired El Paso Corp in 2012 -> Veresen Inc. acquired the other (non-KM) 50% for $1.425bn in 2014 (Hart Energy, 'Veresen Acquires 50% Of Northwest Ruby Pipeline'), later folded into Pembina when Pembina acquired Veresen (2017) -> Ruby Pipeline LLC (both KM's and Pembina's 50% stakes) filed Chapter 11 on March 31, 2022 (PR Newswire: 'a natural gas pipeline joint venture between Kinder Morgan, Inc. and Pembina Pipeline Corporation'; KMI continued operating it through the case) -> Tallgrass MLP Operations, LLC won Ruby at the bankruptcy auction for $282.5 million (East Daley Analytics) and completed the 100% acquisition on/about January 13, 2023 (Pipeline & Gas Journal: 'Tallgrass Completes Ruby Pipeline Acquisition, Adds 682 Miles of Infrastructure to Portfolio' -- 'Tallgrass is now the 100% owner following the completion of this acquisition from Kinder Morgan and Pembina'; Tallgrass's own newsroom release confirms the same close; Wikipedia independently corroborates the $282M bankruptcy sale to 'Tallgrass Energy Partners, a Blackstone Group company'). Three independent origins (Pipeline & Gas Journal trade press, East Daley Analytics -- an independent midstream research firm, and Wikipedia) all agree the CURRENT (since Jan 2023) 100% owner is Tallgrass -- this is now nearly 3.5 years stale on the sheet. Matches the exact naming convention already staged on sibling row P0208 (Tallgrass Interstate Gas Transmission) in this same batch: Owner1='Tallgrass Energy' is the ultimate-parent brand name, distinct from the FERC-certificated operating subsidiary (which stays 'Ruby Pipeline, L.L.C.' in Operator).

validity.recommendation: update SegmentCost -- GEM's $2.96bn is the ORIGINAL (2009) pre-construction estimate; multiple independent sources put the actual/final project cost at roughly $3.5-3.65bn after well-documented 2010-2011 delays and overruns
validity.researcher_notes: GEM's current SegmentCost (2,960,000,000 USD) exactly matches EIA's Historical Natural Gas Pipeline Projects workbook (Cost=2960, same Docket CP09-54 row) -- but that is precisely the problem: both appear to carry forward Ruby's ORIGINAL 2009 FERC-filing-era cost estimate, not the as-built figure. Contemporaneous 2011 reporting documents a specific, sourced cost increase: El Paso Corp. raised its Ruby cost estimate 18% (a $590 million increase) to $3.55 billion in February 2011, citing permitting delays, additional cultural-resource survey/mitigation work, and litigation (Bloomberg, 'El Paso Boosts Ruby Pipeline Cost Estimates, Delays Start,' 2011-02-24 -- could not verify this specific URL directly, blocked 403, but the same $3.55bn figure for the SAME Feb-2011 revised estimate is independently stated by Natural Gas Intelligence's contemporaneous reporting, which I did verify and read directly: 'The $3.55 billion Ruby Pipeline, which has a capacity of 1.5 Bcf/d...'). Oregon Public Broadcasting's 2011 in-service story independently corroborates a cost in the same range: 'Ruby Pipeline To Open After $3.5 Billion And One Year's Work.' A third, independent project-database source (Offshore Technology / formerly Hydrocarbons Technology, a market-intelligence publisher unconnected to El Paso/Kinder Morgan/Tallgrass) states the somewhat higher final figure '$3.65bn' as the total project cost. All three of these independent origins (NGI's 2011 news reporting, OPB's 2011 news reporting, and the Offshore Technology project database) agree the true cost is materially above GEM's $2.96bn -- by 18-23%, well past the >=10%-of-value threshold for a material spec conflict. I'm proposing $3,650,000,000 (the more specific, latest-stated total-investment figure) as the candidate, while flagging in this note that the two 2011-vintage independent sources instead support $3,550,000,000 -- a researcher should pick whichever figure best matches GEM's SegmentCostYear convention (proposal-estimate vs. final-cost) once that column is set. Either way, $2.96bn is stale.

Searched Ruby's current FERC Gas Tariff (pipeline.tallgrassenergylp.com/Content/RUBY/RUBY_tariff.pdf, 184pp, downloaded and read via pdftotext) for a single mainline MAOP/design-pressure figure. The tariff DOES state maximum/minimum pressures, but only per individual receipt/delivery point (e.g. Pearl Creek, Topaz Ridge, Humboldt/Pinyon interconnects), and these vary by point (spot-checked values of 720 psig and 921 psig at different points) rather than stating one system-wide MAOP. No secondary source (Wikipedia, EIA, trade press, FERC EIS notice) states a pipeline-wide design/operating pressure either. Leaving blank rather than picking one point-specific figure and presenting it as the line's pressure -- that would misrepresent a receipt-point-specific MAOP as a system spec.

Per gem_schema.md's FuelSource gotcha, this wants a named upstream field/plant, not 'Natural Gas'. Ruby does not source from one field: it aggregates Rockies-basin gas via multiple receipt-point interconnects clustered around the Opal Hub/Opal Complex in Lincoln County, WY (the tariff's receipt-point table names points like 'Pearl Creek', 'Topaz Ridge', and interconnects with other pipeline systems such as Overthrust, Kern River, Colorado Interstate Gas, and Wyoming Interstate rather than named producing fields). No source names a single dominant upstream field/plant. Leaving blank rather than defaulting to a generic answer (Opal Hub is a delivery/interconnect hub, not a producing field or plant, so it would be a mischaracterization to put it in this field).
